newsitem.title: JAPAN: US, Japan struggle to meet insurance feud deadline.
newsitem.headline: US, Japan struggle to meet insurance feud deadline.

text.p: U.S. and Japanese ministers will meet in Tokyo late next week for a final effort to resolve a drawn-out dispute over Japan's insurance market, but doubts persist over whether they can do so by a December 15 deadline.
Negotiators agreed on Tuesday that Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky and Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka would meet on December 6-7 to try to forge a deal.
"It is very difficult to say that we can reach an agreement at the ministerial meeting, but we will make utmost efforts to resolve the issue," a Finance Ministry official told reporters.
"If there is no agreement on December 6 and 7, it will be close to a breakdown," the official added.

The dispute has become a major irritant in U.S.-Japan trade ties. U.S. President Bill Clinton told Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Sunday that the row was now their most important two-way trade problem. The two met on the fringes of a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders in Manila.

Senior negotiators met in Tokyo on Monday and Tuesday to lay the groundwork for the ministerial talks on the dispute, centring on U.S. charges that Japan is reneging on a 1994 pact on deregulation of its $400 billion insurance market.

Negotiators from both sides said no real progress had been made. Ira Shapiro, senior counsel for the U.S. Trade Representative, and Eisuke Sakakibara, director general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, will meet again ahead of the ministerial talks.

But Shapiro said it was up to the ministers to solve the spat. "We have made no progress resolving these major issues and remain a considerable distance apart," he told a news conference. "The issues will require ministerial attention and discussion, and they'll get that."

Negotiators have already missed one deadline set by Clinton and Hashimoto, who agreed at the June Group of Seven (G7) summit that the feud should be ironed out by July 31. But no agreement was reached and a new deadline was set.

Both sides now say, however, that December 15 is the final target. "The deadline of December 15 was underscored by the president and the prime minister and it's not for me to extend it," Shapiro said. "It won't be extended."
Shapiro and his Japanese counterparts sought to scuttle speculation that Barshefsky and Mitsuzuka might meet again if they failed to forge a deal on December 6-7.

"We've already spent a considerable period of time trying to arrange this meeting," Shapiro said. "So we're focused on this meeting and I think that this is the meeting at which the ministers will make their efforts to resolve the major issues."

But Shapiro declined specific comment on whether Washington would start trade sanction proceedings if no deal was made. "We have said we need to resolve the dispute by December 15 and that we will respond appropriately to things that happen after that if we have not been able to reach an agreement," he said.

Washington has accused Tokyo of reneging on the 1994 pact by moving to open its "third sector" niche insurance market for products such as personal accident and health care policies before freeing up its primary life and non-life sectors.
U.S. insurers like American International Group have a firm foothold in the lucrative third sector.

Japan allowed subsidiaries of domestic life and non-life insurers to start operations in each other's turfs on October 1, but barred them from selling some third-sector products -- stand-alone cancer, hospitalisation, nursing care and personal accident insurance -- before January 1.

Washington also wants Japan to deregulate auto insurance and allow different rates for different categories of drivers. "Auto is key because it represents almost 50 percent of the primary sector non-life side," Shapiro said.
Japan lifted a ban on mail-order sales of auto insurance policies on October 1, but did not change the current system of setting blanket premium rates for auto insurance.
